claims.text: Increasing atomic size mismatch in a lightweight high-entropy alloy induces lattice distortion.
Lattice distortions act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion enhances yield strength.
Lattice distortions restrict oxygen diffusion pathways.
Restricted oxygen diffusion improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Restricted oxygen diffusion improves corrosion resistance.
The proposed increase in strength and environmental resistance can be achieved without a significant density increase.
The modified alloy will have a statistically significant increase in yield strength relative to the baseline.
The modified alloy will have superior oxidation resistance relative to the baseline.
The modified alloy will have superior corrosion resistance relative to the baseline.
The modified alloy will retain a density comparable to that of the baseline alloy.
At temperatures substantially above the design limits, thermal energy may overcome the barrier effects associated with lattice distortion.
Overcoming the lattice-distortion barriers at high temperature will diminish the mechanical-strength benefit.
Overcoming the lattice-distortion barriers at high temperature will diminish oxidation resistance.
Overcoming the lattice-distortion barriers at high temperature will diminish corrosion resistance.
The baseline is defined as a lightweight high-entropy alloy with minimal atomic-size variance among its constituent elements.
Element substitution is proposed to increase atomic-size disparity while preserving low density.
Reduced ductility in the modified alloy would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The uncertainty field treats reduced ductility as a possible unresolved trade-off, whereas the falsification rule declares any reduced ductility sufficient to falsify the hypothesis. Preservation of ductility is not part of the core hypothesis or predicted outcome.
